articles.title: Separation making Alberta master of its destiny ‘a fiction,’ business leader says
articles.summary: With fewer than 45 days to go until the Alberta referendum, a provincial business organization has launched a new initiative intended to make the case for Alberta to remain in Canada.

image.caption: Adam Legge, president of the Business Council of Alberta, pictured in a file photo. Legge says separation would introduce significant uncertainties to the province around trade, market access and more. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
With fewer than 45 days to go until the Alberta referendum, a provincial business organization has launched a new initiative intended to make the case for Alberta to remain in Canada.
Adam Legge says case to remain comes down to certainty as group launches new initiative
With fewer than 45 days to go until the Alberta referendum, few individual business leaders have spoken publicly on the prospect of separation from Canada.
But the leader of an Alberta business organization says that doesn’t mean they aren’t paying close attention.
“There is some hesitancy [to speak out],” Adam Legge, president of the Business Council of Alberta, told reporters Tuesday.
It’s likely that many Alberta companies have employees and customers who would support separation, Legge said.
But he added the majority of the group’s members have spoken “loud and clear” that they want him to speak in favour of remaining in Canada.
The organization’s membership includes more than 130 executives and presidents for top corporations across Alberta’s major sectors.
“They do recognize that if the referendum were to be positive in support of separation, that would create a massive amount of uncertainty,” Legge said.
On Tuesday, the council launched a new website, along with a series of videos and graphics, intended to make the case for Alberta to remain in Canada.
A significant number of members, particularly in the resource sector, have long been frustrated with federal policy, Legge said.
While he said the status quo is not a path forward, sentiment has been changing in the wake of recent developments, like Alberta's proposed oil pipeline to the West Coast.
And factors that will determine if separation were to be positive or negative, like trade agreements, market access, currency and interest rates, are mostly outside Alberta’s control, Legge said.
“The notion that a separate Alberta would be a master of its own destiny is a fiction,” he said.
Legge sat on the provincial "Alberta Next" panel last summer, which held a series of in-person town halls across the province with the stated goal of devising ways to increase provincial autonomy.

The Business Council of Alberta said it isn’t registering as a third-party advertiser for the upcoming referendum, but will continue to produce content to post on its website and social media channels.
More groups expected to weigh in
The Business Council of Alberta isn’t the only major business organization to draw a line in the sand when it comes to separation.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: In June, a report released by the Calgary Chamber of Commerce suggested separation could spur a business exodus and shrink the provincial economy by $62 billion a year.
Last week, the Canada West Foundation, a public policy think tank, said though Alberta’s grievances with Ottawa may be real, separation would be too costly and pose too many uncertainties.
Independence groups have suggested such projections assume “worst-case outcomes” and ignore Alberta’s leverage.
Last week, the pro-independence Alberta Transition Council, led by lawyer Keith Wilson, released a 214-page report laying out a “transition plan” should Alberta become its own country.
Wilson has said the nature of Alberta’s economy is immobile, meaning the province would be in a solid negotiating position in the event of a “yes” vote.

“They cannot relocate our natural resources, our expansive agricultural production, our oil and gas,” Wilson said last week. “We’re in a much stronger position, not only to negotiate with the rest of Canada, but also with the United States.”
Even more analyses on the prospect of Alberta separation are anticipated, including a University of Calgary study, expected to be released this month.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Joel is a reporter/editor with CBC Calgary. In fall 2021, he spent time with CBC's bureau in Lethbridge. He was previously the editor of the Airdrie City View and Rocky View Weekly newspapers. He hails from Swift Current, Sask. Reach him by email at joel.dryden@cbc.ca

articles.title: Far-right port protests: police told to improve intelligence gathering
articles.summary:
Whitehall officials also ask why laws meant to clamp down on the wearing of masks at demonstrations were not used

Police have been told by the government they expect better intelligence…

blocks.text: Police have been told by the government they expect better intelligence gathering after masked far-right groups took to the streets at the weekend, the Guardian has learned, as the Kent force admitted mishandling warnings of potential trouble.
Police in Kent on Saturday and then Portsmouth, Hampshire, on Sunday said they were taken by surprise when hundreds massed to oppose what they say is illegal immigration via small boats.
Both protests are believed by police to have been far-right inspired, with evidence emerging that those behind them were determined to avoid detection.
Claims by Kent police since Saturday that they had no warning fell apart on Tuesday when the force admitted there were warning calls to police on Friday evening which were not acted upon.
Kent police said: “The force had received non-emergency information late on Friday evening that a protest could take place in the town the following day. This information was not fully assessed.”
The government’s view is that police actions once officers were faced by hundreds of men was reasonable.

But there is dismay at how Kent police explained their decision making afterwards, for instance viewing the gathered masked men outside the port of Dover as peaceful protesters, with one source describing it as “fucking crackers”.
On Tuesday evening the prime minister, Andy Burnham, met police chiefs to discuss what had happened and preparedness for any further unrest.
In Dover on Saturday, where hundreds of masked men in black converged undetected, police believe those taking to the streets used walkie-talkies to coordinate their actions.

Police on the ground report the masked men had lawyers’ phone numbers and cited public order case law and were well briefed on how far they could go: “They toed the line perfectly to avoid arrest”, one source said.
In Hampshire police are investigating whether vehicles were deliberately left behind to block access roads.
Police said the Dover gathering passed peacefully, while in Hampshire there were clashes, with the local Police Federation saying anger and violence was directed at officers.
The Guardian understands that part of Hampshire police’s investigation will examine whether the gathering of 200 people was meant to harass or intimidate.
A spokesperson added they are also hunting for those behind the violence, conducting “a thorough review of the body-worn video” to look for offenders.
The protests are believed to have been co-ordinated on closed social media networks and not publicly advertised.

Police are considering whether the threshold for warrants for covert tactics has been met, with one source warning that police were wary of criticism of using “police state tactics” against people portraying themselves as peaceful protesters motivated by a legitimate issue.
The National Police Coordination Centre has intensified its monitoring.

The action in Kent was organised by Daniel Thomas, a long-term associate of the far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known as Tommy Robinson. Thomas, who has established an umbrella grouping called Patriot Platform, was also linked to the blockade in Portsmouth the following day.
Whitehall officials have asked police why tougher laws in place since last year meant to clamp down on the wearing of face masks at protests were not used.

The police view was that at Dover those gathered complied with requests from officers and dispersed after three hours. In Portsmouth, which was more heated, police prioritised a formal dispersal order which they think worked.
Both police and government sources say the “optics”, of masked men in black thronging the streets, looked “intimidating”.

Also on Tuesday it emerged that lifeboat staff who picked up 120 asylum seekers from a large dinghy in the Channel on Sunday were refused entry to two ports shortly before being harangued by right-wing protesters.
Crew on two RNLI vessels were also threatened with legal action if they approached Southampton Port and tried to bring the claimants ashore.

They were forced to take the migrants several miles away to Eastney, where police, firefighters, Border Force and other officials faced protests by up to 200 people, most of whom wore balaclavas and black clothing.
Peter Sparkes, the chief executive of the RNLI, said abuse of its volunteers is “wholly unacceptable in a civilised society”.
He said recent protests had “generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding” about the charity, and condemned threats by “those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard”.
Officials confirmed that a broadcast on an open marine VHF radio said that Southampton Vessel Traffic Service and King’s Harbour Master Portsmouth denied the RNLI permission to enter their ports.
The two RNLI rescue boats from Bembridge and Yarmouth had intercepted a “mega-dinghy” that had left Utah beach near Cherbourg in Normandy.

A spokesperson for Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates the port of Southampton, told the Guardian: “ABP did receive an inquiry about landing recovered migrants at the port of Southampton. We had to decline the inquiry as the port did not have suitable reception facilities available. If there had been a safety of life at sea issue where Southampton was the closest port or if we had received a formal direction from the relevant authority then we would have played a role. Neither was the case in this situation.”

On Tuesday, anti-illegal-migrant protesters attempted to identify RNLI volunteers involved in rescuing those onboard the dinghy. Demonstrators named and shared pictures on X of two people they said were volunteers, claiming they had tracked down an address for one of the men.

Sparkes’s words come after footage posted on social media showed volunteers labelled as “traitors”. In a statement issued on Tuesday, Sparkes said the misinformation led to “some of our volunteers and staff [being] the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse.
“The RNLI’s people represent the very best in our society. They selflessly give up their time to keep others safe.
“Yet they and their families are being threatened by those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard.
“Their action, in contrast, is wholly unacceptable in a civilised society.
“We will take whatever steps we can to care for and protect our people and their families.”

articles.title: Otto Jelinek, Canadian figure skating world champion and Olympian, dead at 86
articles.summary: Otto Jelinek, a former world-champion figure skater and federal cabinet minister, has died at the age of 86.

image.caption: Former Canadian Olympian and federal cabinet minister Otto Jelinek spent 21 years in Parliament. (Jonathan Hayward/Canadian Press/File)

blocks.text: New
Otto Jelinek, a former world-champion figure skater and federal cabinet minister, has died at the age of 86.
Ex-cabinet minister lived with Parkinson's disease for nearly 20 years, his brother says
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 08, 2026 2:56 PM EDT | Last Updated: 4 minutes ago

"He was quite the ambitious guy," his younger brother Henry said Sunday, a day after Jelinek's death. "He was also sincerely and strongly a Canadian guy, who did everything he could to help this country."
Jelinek was born in Prague in 1940, and his family fled Czechoslovakia's communist government, arriving in Canada in 1952.
His father owned a successful cork factory in Prague and later rebuilt it in Oakville, Ont., a town between Toronto and Hamilton.
Jelinek and his sister Maria represented Canada in paired figure skating at the 1960 Winter Olympics in California.

In 1962, the pair won an emotional gold medal back in Prague, as champions of world figure skating. Henry said his siblings made the family proud by disproving the communist regime's propaganda of being the best system in the world.
The pair toured with the Ice Capades entertainment show while Jelinek became a sports commentator for CTV. He also started a company manufacturing hockey and figure skates.

In 1972, Jelinek entered federal politics, representing a Toronto riding before switching to the Oakville area. His 21 years in Parliament included a term as national revenue minister under then Prime Minister Brian Mulroney, as well as portfolios in sport and multiculturalism.
Jelinek described himself as politically right-of-centre, and he said he had been involved in backroom politics during the era of former Prime Minister John Diefenbaker.
Otto Jelinek to Canadian athletes: The buck stops here
Minister of amateur sport in 1984
As a young MP, buried deep in the Tory opposition benches during the 1970s, Jelinek baited Liberal Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau as a closet communist.
When the Tories swept to power in 1984, Jelinek became minister of amateur sport, later adding multiculturalism, public works, and supply and services to his resume.
In 1989 he became revenue minister, implementing and defending the GST while fighting an uphill battle against cross-border shopping.

items: Skate Canada says former Olympic figure skater Alexandra Paul killed in 2023 car crash
Denis Ten's death leaves figure skating community devastated

blocks.text: Jelinek once remarked that he would make a poor diplomat because he speaks his mind too easily, such as in 1991 when he suggested the Tory government may have taxed Canadians too aggressively, earning him the wrath of some cabinet colleagues.
"I have a view on everything," he told Hill reporters in 1993, such as saying Canada's multiculturalism policy "has played its role" and should be shelved.
"I for one resent being referred to as a hyphenated Canadian. I believe we have to get rid of hyphenated Canadians," he told reporters in a scrum.
Jelinek also said it was unfair Ottawa spends so much on health care "just because every time a little kid has a runny nose the mother takes him to a doctor."
That year, Jelinek was shuffled out of cabinet and he said he would not seek election.
Jelinek announced his eventual retirement from politics to reporters, saying he had told his riding executive he would run for the party leadership only 24 hours prior.

"I was set to go until I ran into these guys -- my wife and my two boys, aged 10 and five years old. And suddenly life's reality hit home," Jelinek was quoted saying in a Canadian Press report, which noted his voice was cracking, with tears welling up in his eyes.
Refused to testify to Parliament
"It hit right where it counts, in the heart. Because these children have been growing up with a part-time father."

After politics, Jelinek took a job with a company that partnered with a firm that won the right to operate part of Pearson International Airport in Toronto, a move he said complied with conflict-of-interest rules.

The privatization of the airport was cancelled and became a major election issue. In 1994, Jelinek was among those who refused to testify to Parliament about the cancelled deal. The Bloc Quebecois at the time threatened to subpoena him and others.
Jelinek later moved to the Czech Republic and launched a consultancy in Prague, focused on helping Canadian and U.S. businesses get established in eastern Europe. He returned to Canada to retire.

In 2013, then-Prime Minister Stephen Harper appointed Jelinek as Canadian Ambassador to the Czech Republic. The role included overseeing the lifting of visa requirements for Czech nations, which had become a thorny issue that threatened to derail a free trade-agreement with the European Union.
Henry Jelinek said the family marveled that they went from fleeing communism to having Jelinek represent Canada as ambassador in the country of his birth.
Jelinek said his brother spent much of his retirement alongside Lake Ontario, where he loved gardening, golf, tennis, Frank Sinatra songs and parties.
"He loves to tell stories which he often exaggerates a little bit," Henry Jelinek said. "If somebody would need something, he would be there, always."

Jelinek died peacefully Saturday at the Trillium Health Centre in Mississauga, Ont., after living with Parkinson's disease for nearly 20 years, his brother said. "He took it with great heroism and dignity, to the very end."

articles.title: German economy frets about Saxony-Anhalt election results
articles.summary: The AfD won the election in the eastern German state by a wide margin. While politicians and election analysts are still debating the reasons for the far-right party's popularity, economists are…

image.caption: Good spirits at the AfD election party: AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel stands with with winning candidate Ulrich SiegmundImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The results came in as predicted: The AfD, which is considered far-right extremist in parts, won the election in Saxony-Anhalt and could now put forward the state’s minister-president and take over the state government.

What hardly anyone expected, however, was this: The governing CDU is now barely half as strong as it was, while the other parties have been left far behind. Calling it a landslide victory for the AfD is no exaggeration. And many commentators go so far as to call it a turning point in Germany’s postwar history.
Keep calm and carry on?

"A state government led by the AfD would certainly be seen by many as a turning point and would further fuel the debate over how best to deal with the party," Commerzbank economist Ralph Solveen told Reuters.
At the same time, he advises waiting to see what happens, saying that things are rarely as bad as they seem.

"Many of these decisions are unlikely to affect the economy until the medium to long term," he said. "Decisions on most taxes, the structure of the labor market and social security systems are made at the federal level. That is why the AfD, in many of its pledges, only promises to advocate for something in the Bundesrat, which is unlikely to succeed given the foreseeable isolation of an AfD-led government."
What next after far-right AfD win in regional election?
Local political pragmatism?
Many business community concerns had already been raised before the election. It also became clear that there are differing views within the AfD, which could lead to unpredictable policies.

For example, DW reported two months ago that Hannes Loth, a member of the AfD and the mayor in Raguhn-Jessnitz, Saxony-Anhalt, sought to have six new wind turbines installed. This pledge puts him at odds with the official stance of his own party.

Whether this is a sign of internal party pluralism or simply local political pragmatism will become clear during the coming legislative term, especially if the AfD ends up in the state government. It is not, however, serving to reassure business leaders.
Consequences of xenophobia

One issue the AfD campaigned on was a promise to limit the number of foreigners. But will the party actually be able to implement its goal? On this point, Michael Berlemann, director of the Hamburg Institute of International Economics (HWWI), remains skeptical.

"A large part of the measures it has promised cannot be implemented at the state level because the federal government is responsible for them," he said. "Another part would be illegal and would be overturned by the courts after some delay: The AfD cannot restrict the immigration of foreign skilled workers in Saxony-Anhalt."

ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski pointed to the national shortage of skilled workers: "Forced deportations in Saxony-Anhalt would probably be limited. However, the symbolic effect cannot be underestimated. As with Trump, such headlines would act as a deterrent for foreign skilled workers."
Wido Geis-Thöne, an economist at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, sees it the same way.

He told DW that the AfD would "do everything in its power to pursue its migration policy goals." However, it could only "do things that actually fall under the responsibility of the state rather than the federal government."
Economic fallout for Saxony-Anhalt

Geis-Thöne said the state itself would be the main victim of such a policy: "With an anti-immigration state government, Saxony-Anhalt will become significantly less attractive a destination for foreign skilled workers, regardless of whether anything actually changes for them from a legal perspective."

For HWWI Director Berlemann, the indirect impacts of the AfD's plans are particularly problematic. The measures announced would mean "that many skilled workers who are particularly needed in health care and nursing, hospitality and tourism, the food industry and agriculture and in construction and logistics will avoid the state in the future."
This would exacerbate the shortage of skilled workers and widen the state's economic gap.
Openness and diversity are key

Saxony-Anhalt must remain a state where people from around the world want to live and work and where companies want to invest and new technologies can emerge, Bitkom President Ralf Wintergerst warned.

He told the Catholic News Agency KNA: "The digital economy thrives on openness, diversity and international cooperation. Companies invest where they find good conditions and where skilled workers from Germany and abroad are welcomed."

Regarding foreign investment, ING Chief Economist Carsten Brzeski told Reuters: "Sure, there could be a symbolic effect on foreign investors. But let's not forget: Saxony-Anhalt is not the entire German economy."
What the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt win means for Germany
How should Berlin react
DIW President Marcel Fratzscher painted a bleak picture of the economic future after the Saxony-Anhalt election.

"Regardless of the makeup of the next state government, a controversial or weak government and the polarization during the election campaign are likely to accelerate the departure of people and companies from Saxony-Anhalt, thereby significantly worsening conditions in the state," he said.

He told Reuters that the election result was "above all a vote of no confidence in the federal government." The consequence, he added, must be "that the federal government changes course and implements far-reaching structural reforms involving subsidies, bureaucracy, taxes, the social security system and Europe."

Tanja Gönner, managing director of the Federation of German Industries (BDI), took a similar perspective. Following the state election, she called on the federal government to be single-minded in pursuing a reform agenda.
"The response to this state election result must not be political paralysis at the federal level," she said.

The federal government must now consistently implement and expand reforms to boost investment, innovation and growth, she told RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland, adding that "the positions of radical parties are not suitable for this."

The political center must now show that it is capable of taking action, BDI's managing director said, adding that what is needed is a policy focused on competitiveness and growth at both the state and federal levels. A single state election result must not distract from that goal, she concluded.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Ed Miliband has overturned decades of Foreign Office inertia on illegal Israeli settlements
articles.summary:
Foreign secretary ends UK’s feigned helplessness with sanctions and description of Israel’s actions as ethnic cleansing

The indefatigable ability of UK Foreign Office ministers over decades…

blocks.text: The indefatigable ability of UK Foreign Office ministers over decades to issue boilerplate statements of concern about the extension of illegal settlements in Israel has long been a matter of ridicule.

Even some of the Conservative ministers who issued them, notably Alan Duncan and Alistair Burt, have agreed. Duncan described the UK stance towards settlements as weak and naive, while Burt wondered at the ability of the Foreign Office to find new forms of diplomatic condemnation that never amounted to any specific action. Margaret Thatcher, often torn as prime minister between her natural sympathy for Israel and her fear of the Gulf states falling under the sway of the Soviet Union, similarly expressed her anger at the settlements.

But in the face of the Israeli disillusionment with a two-state solution – to which the UK had been committed at the UN since 1946, if not before – the UK produced little practical policy to prevent the spread of Israel’s illegal settlements.

The UK-Israel trade agreement prevented preferential tariffs applying to goods coming from territories brought under Israeli administration after June 1967. The business department also advised companies not to trade with the settlements – but many simply ignored the advice or, to secure the preferential tariff, relabelled their goods as from Israel. The then trade minister Chris Bryant told the business select committee in June it was very difficult to be certain of the origin of goods.
At the same time, the legal advice was the UK regime could sanction entities only if they were linked to settler violence, but could not sanction a contractor for simply working on settlements.

blocks.caption: Young Palestinians look at a new Israeli settlement from the Palestinian village of Duma, near Nablus, in the Israeli-occupied West Bankin February 2026. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: It was this unhappy moral and legal mess that Ed Miliband inherited. As soon as he took office as foreign secretary, he said he refused to be a bystander to further suffering and the destruction of the two-state solution that settlement expansion represented. In this he had the support of the prime minister, Andy Burnham.

Above all, Miliband felt that the UK could not feign powerlessness, and to do so, or pay lip service to action, would prove disastrous to Israel’s own future. He was perhaps the only front rank Labour politician that could push this argument through at such pace, overturning the inertia and caution built into Foreign Office legal advice.

His Jewish heritage – his mother, Marion Kozak, was a holocaust survivor who fled to Israel – his life growing up with the Palestinian question and empathy for those subjected to antisemitism put him in a near unimpeachable position to adopt the role of Israel’s critical friend. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, might this week say the Labour government is gripped by Jew-hatred, a charge he laid at Miliband’s door knowing he is Jewish, but Miliband’s riposte is simple. The best route to Israel’s security lay in Palestinian self-determination and the introduction of the two-state solution in its fullest form. To equate Israel only with the current Likud-led government as too many Conservatives have been prone to do was a category error, he said: “Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, plain and simple.”

He is thus the first UK foreign secretary to describe what is happening in the West Bank as ethnic cleansing, and in so doing to in effect accuse Israel of turning a blind eye to acts that amount to war crimes.

Miliband also ended the two years of delay in responding to the International Court of Justice advisory opinion in June 2024 that the occupation is unlawful. In what he admitted was an overdue statement of reality, he accepted the ICJ opinion that the occupation, and not just the settlements, were so designated. Accepting the ICJ opinion arguably places stronger obligations on the UK government to not assist the occupation. It may help to explain why the trade ban extends into services such as providing insurance for illegal settlements.

blocks.caption: Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel and a steadfast supporter of the Netanyahu government, has previously claimed that Ed Miliband hates Jews. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The biggest diplomatic rabbit Miliband pulled from the hat was the agreement of France and Canada to impose similar trade bans. France took the lead last year on recognition of Palestine; this year, it is the turn of the UK to lead on following through on the consequences of that recognition.

Paris appears to have been persuaded by the UK to stop waiting for the EU to reach an agreement on collective action, since it seemed unlikely the opposition in Germany and indifference in parts of the European Commission would end. A group of countries imposing the trade ban together of course makes Israeli reprisals harder, and serves to underline Israel’s isolation.
The perceived weaknesses are obvious.

Miliband still left it to the international courts to determine whether a genocide occurred in Gaza, something that might not be adjudicated for at least five years. There was mounting evidence of ethnic cleansing in Gaza, he said, but again it was for the courts to determine if that is so.

There is no pledge to protect the International Court of Justice or the International Criminal Court from the US drive to render them inoperable. As to a UK arms sales ban, an exemption continues for the sale of parts for F35 jet planes to the main US spares pool – all on the basis the F-35 jets “do not materially support the occupation” – the criteria the foreign secretary has set.

Miliband specifically condemned the Boycott, Disinvestment and Sanctions movement because it targets the whole Israeli economy and not just the occupied territories. The secondary legislation required to make sanctions as wide as envisaged may take as long as nine months, contrasting with the speed with which sanctions were enforced against Russia over the annexation of Crimea.

But to focus solely on what is absent is to miss the moment. Duncan, for instance, said: “At last, in the face of state-backed terrorism by illegal settlers, the British government has shown unprecedented moral courage.”

There is a risk of a cascading backlash from the White House – but Trump, trapped in a political labyrinth after he was persuaded to attack Iran, has little reason to come to Benjamin Netanyahu’s aid. Miliband has taken a risk, but after more than 70,000 deaths in Gaza, and the two-state solution on life support, it may be time to dare.

articles.title: UK to force Apple and Google to block explicit images on children’s smartphones
articles.summary:
Lisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthrough

Apple and Google will be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK…

blocks.text: Apple and Google will be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said.
The legislation commitment puts ministers on a collision course with two of the biggest players in Silicon Valley, months after the government announced a social media ban for under-16s.

Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, said the government would start work on an act of parliament to stop under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.
Talks with Google and Apple, whose operating systems dominate the smartphone market, had not reached agreement as a three-month deadline passed on Tuesday.
Nandy told the House of Commons the tech companies could still reach a deal but it was “almost certain” groundbreaking legislation would be required.

“For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from some of the worst harms,” she said. “And to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace that we need it to, while harm is being done now.”

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the protections would be “built into the device and switched on by default”, and tech companies will be required to verify an adult user’s age before they are allowed to take, view or send nude images. The government also wants the restrictions to apply to apps used by children, which will require further legislation.
Nandy said: “This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world.”
Sources familiar with progress in the talks have said there iwas a desire to reach a deal on both sides but significant hurdles remained including privacy concerns on the tech side.

Jess Phillips, the Labour MP and former safeguarding minister, said the legislation would stop the UK from producing self-generated child sexual abuse material, where children are duped or groomed into sharing explicit images of themselves.
However, she urged the government to ensure the UK was followed by other countries and to make sure that “while we lead the world, we’re not standing alone for too long”.

Hannah Swirsky, head of policy at the Internet Watch Foundation, which monitors the online spread of child sexual abuse material [CSAM], said: “It is deeply disappointing that tech firms have failed to act in full, but we are pleased that the government is now taking decisive legislative action to keep children safe.”
Last year the IWF said a quarter of the images or videos of CSAM it recorded were self-generated, representing more than 140,000 pieces of content over a 12-month period.

One of Keir Starmer’s final acts as prime minister was to give Apple and Google three months to stop under-18s from generating, sending or seeing nude images on their devices, by activating built-in features on the hardware or other technological solutions. Between them, Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android smartphone operating systems dominate the mobile phone market.
The nudity block implies the use of “client-side scanning”, where content is scanned by software on the device before it is encrypted or sent.

“Client-side scanning is the least evil approach,” said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow in cybersecurity and privacy at Kings College London. “That said, it does put in place an infrastructure to scan content of messages.”

Privacy campaigners have also warned that adults would have to verify their age before switching off any nudity-blocking features. In June, the government said the proposals would “not affect the use of devices owned and used by adults who verify their age”.

Google said it was “pleased to have made progress” in talks with the government and was “fully committed” to working with legislators, experts, app developers and device manufacturers to “keep children safe, while also protecting privacy and access to information”.
An Apple spokesperson said the company was preparing to strengthen its “communication safety” feature, which warns children when they are receiving or sending nude images and videos.

“We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen communication safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe.”

articles.title: South Park changes name to South America in response to Trump changes
articles.summary:
Satirical program’s new title is ‘inspired by bravery and patriotism’ of Apple and Google, who capitulated to Trump’s requests to change Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’

In light of

blocks.text: In light of Donald Trump’s attempts to rename a gulf, lakes and even states after “America”, South Park, the animated satirical program that has long skewered those in power, has announced an official name change. For its 29th season, the Comedy Central series will be known as “South America”.

“Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA,” creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker said in a statement. “We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount – a Skydance Capitulation.” The show’s parent company, Paramount Skydance, owned by Trump ally David Ellison, is poised to become one of the biggest media conglomerates in the US after the Trump administration approved its $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery (WBD), drawing much creative industry backlash.

The tongue-in-cheek news comes a day after the US president suggested on social media that the state of New Mexico should be renamed “New America” with an AI-generated video that depicted him placing the word “America” over “Mexico” on a “welcome to New Mexico” sign. (The US federal government has no authority to change a state’s name.) The post drew swift condemnation from Democrats, who accused him of trying to distract from his war in Iran and rising prices.

The renaming brouhaha is now a standard Trump move, dating back to the early hours of his second term, when he moved to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”. Last month, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, the administration tried to do the same with Lake Ontario, pushing to relabel it “Lake America”.

The Emmy-winning, gleefully offensive comedy series, which first aired in 1997, has long been a thorn in the Trump administration’s side, as one of the few programs to successfully ridicule and ambitiously poke at an administration often resistant to satire. Creators Parker and Stone have repeatedly drawn ire from Trump and other Maga figures for, among other things, depicting Trump naked in bed with Satan, showing an animated Trump with small genitalia and portraying former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem as a puppy killer whose Botoxed face occasionally melts off.

In August, a writer for the show announced that he purchased the rights to trumpkennedycenter.org, predicting that Trump would change the name of the Kennedy Center after he purged the leadership of the arts institution, installed himself as chair and stocked the board with loyalists.

articles.title: Canada, U.K., France to ban trade of goods from Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Canada, Britain and France say they will ban the trade of goods with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The U.K. is going a step further by implementing fresh sanctions and saying it will…

image.caption: An Israeli settler works at a winery at the settlement of Yitzhar in the occupied West Bank, south of the Palestinian city of Nablus, on Tuesday. The U.K. government says it will implement a comprehensive trade ban and targeted sanctions on goods and services from Israeli settlements in the occupied

blocks.text: World·New

Canada, Britain and France say they will ban the trade of goods with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The U.K. is going a step further by implementing fresh sanctions and saying it will take additional action against companies and individuals that support settlement expansion.
Israel to close British consulate in East Jerusalem in response to joint trade measures
In a packed British Parliament Tuesday, MPs gathered to listen to the government reset its relationship with Israel.

Nodding alongside his cabinet ministers, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who came to power seven weeks ago, listened intently as his equally new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, himself Jewish, announced a ban on settler trade from the occupied West Bank. He said Canada and France would take similar actions.
"Today, France and Canada are announcing alongside Britain that they will also ban the import of goods from illegal settlements," Miliband said.
Cheers echoed through the parliamentary chamber. Miliband noted the three countries are not alone in taking action against Israel’s continued expansion of settlements in the occupied West Bank.

"The Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway, which have either banned goods or are in the process of doing so, with many other countries, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal and Sweden, [are] pledging today they will support further action."
Miliband said the U.K. will also take action "against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate for settlement expansion."
To another loud round of cheers, he said: "You will face the full force of U.K. sanctions."

Miliband said the U.K.'s action was coming now because Israel had crossed a "long-term red line," in reference to its recent announcement that it had opened tenders for construction of 1,200 settler homes in an area known as E1 in the occupied West Bank.

items: As Canada recognizes a Palestinian state, some in the West Bank fear it's too late

blocks.text: The United Nations and most countries deem the settlements illegal under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention pertaining to military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the area as disputed rather than occupied and approving some settlement building.
It is nearly a year since Canada, the U.K. and France announced their governments would recognize the state of Palestine.
A sharp rise in reported violence in the occupied West Bank was another reason the U.K. had decided on sanctions, Miliband said.
"The British government," Miliband told parliamentarians, "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists."

items: Israeli settler blockades part of escalating violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank

blocks.text: Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused his British counterpart of "outrageous lies."

Sa'ar said Israel would undertake countermeasures, including expelling U.K. representatives from a joint military centre monitoring the Gaza ceasefire and ending U.K. training of the Palestinian Authority's security forces in the West Bank.

In addition, Israel will close Britain's consulate in East Jerusalem and prevent the entry into Israel of 12 elected U.K. officials, as well as other British citizens Sa'ar said were "involved in antisemitic and anti-Israel activity."
The seeds of change in the U.K.’s relationship with Israel were evident months ago.

In the days before Burnham became prime minister in July, he indicated a reset. He apologized for the governing Labour Party’s initial response to Israel’s military action in Gaza, saying the party "didn’t get it right" and under his leadership needs to "do better."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Anna Cunningham is a freelance correspondent in London, England. She has reported for the CBC since 2009, and was previously based in Mumbai, Paris and Lagos, Nigeria.

articles.title: Bill allowing former gov’t employees to contribute to GSIS approved
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former government employees in the non-career service may soon be allowed to continue their membership with the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) by making voluntary…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former government employees in the non-career service may soon be allowed to continue their membership with the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) by making voluntary premium contributions, as the House approved a bill seeking to amend a 1997 law.
During the session on Tuesday, the House Bill (HB) No. 10744 was approved on third and final reading after 220 members present voted in the affirmative, with zero negative votes and abstentions.
HB No. 10744 seeks to amend Republic Act No. 8291, or the Government Service Insurance System Act of 1997, by inserting phrases into Section 13, which deals with retirement benefits.

If enacted, Section 13 will include a phrase which states that “members in the non-career service, as defined in Section 9, Chapter 2, Subtitle a, Title I, Book V, of Executive Order (EO) No. 292 […] may continue paying premium contributions to the GSIS” so that they may be qualified for “retirement and other applicable benefits.”
The Civil Service Commission has said on its site that Section 9 of EO No. 292 states that individuals in the non-career service are characterized as:

items: those who enter on bases other than those of the usual tests of merit and fitness utilized for the career service

those whose tenure is limited to a period specified by law, or which is coterminous with that of the appointing authority or subject to his pleasure, or which is limited to the duration of a particular project for which purpose employment was made.

blocks.text: A new subsection in Section 13 will also be created if the bill is signed into law, which sets guidelines on how former employees in the non-career service can qualify for a continuing membership with GSIS.

“A former or separated member in the non-career service who has not completed the required fifteen (15) years of service to qualify for retirement benefits under this act may be allowed to continue paying the full premium contributions, representing both the personal and government shares, until such member has completed the minimum creditable service required for retirement benefits,” the proposed Section 13-B read.
“The payment of voluntary contributions under this section shall be subject to actuarial, administrative, and documentary requirements as may be prescribed by

the GSIS. Provided, however, that the GSIS may allow a member to pay premiums based on a lower salary grade or compensation rate, under reasonable terms and conditions, to provide flexibility and affordability on the part of the member,” it added.

The call to allow GSIS members who have not completed the minimum service requirement due to the nature of their work to continue making contributions — so that they can receive benefits upon retirement—is not new.

In February 2023, former Senator Aquilino “Koko” Pimentel called for a change in the policy in terms of availing pensions for retired local officials and their staff who did not meet the GSIS’ 15-year minimum service requirement.

Pimentel highlighted the disparity between the minimum requirement and the term limits of elected officials, as he revealed that many temporary and co-terminus government officials and employees retire without a pension program due to the 15-year minimum service requirement of the social insurance institution.
Co-terminus officials fall under the category of non-career service employees.

“I appeal for our local officials and their staff who have served nine years in government but cannot qualify for the pension program due to the 15-year minimum service requirement under Republic Act 8291,” he said in a statement on February 26, 2023.

“I am saddened to learn that there are so many elected officials and public servants holding temporary and co-terminus status on the national and local levels who would retire without a retirement fund and pension only because they have not met the 15-year minimum service requirement,” he added. /cb

articles.title: More than 600 flights in and out of U.K. cancelled due to air traffic control issue
articles.summary: More than 600 flights were cancelled on Tuesday due to a technical issue in Britain's air traffic control system that caused disruptions at major airports across the U.K., the flight monitoring…

image.caption: Stranded passengers gather after some departing flights were cancelled at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 5 in London on Tuesday. Several major British airports were disrupted after air traffic control provider NATS experienced a technical issue. (Isabel Infantes/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

More than 600 flights were cancelled on Tuesday due to a technical issue in Britain's air traffic control system that caused disruptions at major airports across the U.K., the flight monitoring website Flightradar24 reported.
Officials said a technical issue was identified and a fix is underway

Britain's National Air Traffic Services (NATS) said a problem had been identified in its flight processing system and that engineers were urgently working on the issue, which affected flights across the U.K.
In an update, NATS said it had "implemented a fix and our flight system is starting to recover."

At least 625 flights to and from U.K. airports, including London Heathrow, were cancelled, affecting services operated by multiple airlines, such as British Airways, EasyJet, KLM and Lufthansa, according to Flightradar24.

Some passengers took to social media to complain about being stuck on the tarmac for hours before their flights were eventually cancelled. Many expressed frustration about a lack of communication from airlines.

The affected airports included Stansted and City in London, as well as those in Manchester, Birmingham, Gatwick and Scotland. They warned passengers to check the status of their flight with their airline.
Budget airline EasyJet said some of its flights were "unable to operate" and that the system failure caused "delays to flights across Europe."
Heathrow's website showed that many short-haul flights departing for European destinations had been cancelled or delayed.
It was not immediately clear what caused the technical problem.

articles.title: UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response
articles.summary: Britain's foreign secretary accuses settlers of carrying out the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians, as Israel responds by shutting the UK consulate in East Jerusalem.

blocks.text: The sanctions were launched alongside France and Canada, who in a joint statement with the UK said the action "marks a further turning point in our approach to protecting the two-state solution".
Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.
In a statement to MPs, Miliband said: "The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.
"And all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians."
He said ethnic cleansing was defined by the UN as a "purposeful policy designed by one ethnic or religious group to remove by violent means another ethnic or religious from certain areas".

Miliband said the official view of the government was that the Israeli occupation of the West Bank was unlawful because of the "entrenchment of its control, its intention to extend permanent sovereignty, and its expansionist agenda via illegal settlements".
This position, Miliband said, should be reflected in the UK's "economic relationship" with the occupied West Bank.
As a result, over the next six to nine months, the UK will introduce "a new comprehensive sanctions regime", he said.
The foreign secretary also announced a ban on advertising illegal West Bank settlements in the UK.
"The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel," Miliband added.
Later on Tuesday Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the targeted measures were "aimed not at the Israeli people, but in support of the two-state solution".
Announcing the closure of the UK consulate, which represents the UK government in Jerusalem, West Bank and Gaza, Saar said at a press conference: "We know that we have many friends in Britain.
"Unfortunately, we have a hostile Labour government that is consistently operating against the State of Israel, and it has left us no choice but to respond to its hostile actions."
He added that 11 UK MPs, including Jeremy Corbyn, Diane Abbott and all five sitting Green Party MPs, would be banned from entering Israel, accusing them of "antisemitic and anti-Israel activity".
The UK also issued a joint statement with 11 other countries; France, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden.
It said the group was unequivocally committed to the two-state solution and would introduce national measures or support European restrictions on trading goods with West Bank settlements.

The UK announcement comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation. Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure.

Miliband told the Commons the UK's "new approach" was necessary because plans for the E1 development in the West Bank would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
Elsewhere, he said war crimes "appear to have been committed" in Gaza in the years since the 7 October attack on Israel in 2023.

He said: "International humanitarian law imposes clear rules for states fighting wars, including to ensure access to food and medical supplies, to avoid mass displacement of civilians, and to avoid the targeting of civilians. Serious and international violations of this law, if proven, amount to war crimes.
"What has occurred, including the actions of the IDF, have been examined in depth by a number of organisations, including the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry.
"The conclusions of these reports represent increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed, and we support legal processes to determine this."
He added it was up to international courts to determine if Israel has committed a genocide in Gaza.
Israel's leaders have consistently rejected allegations of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. They have insisted that Israeli forces have operated in accordance with international law.
Miliband began his statement to the Commons by referring to his Jewish roots and childhood experiences of visiting Israel, as well as recent antisemitic attacks in the UK.
He described himself as "a proud British Jew" and outlined his steadfast support for the state of Israel.

He said: "My personal story and that of thousands of British Jews is one of the many reasons why I say to anyone here or around the world who questions Israel's right to exist as a homeland for the Jewish people - you are wrong, and we will call you out whenever you engage in this attempt at the erasure of Israel."

But the UK's Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was a "truly a dark day for British Jews", saying the sanctions were "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric" that would embolden people who "use hatred as a weapon against Jews".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews expressed "deep regret" over Tuesday's announcement, and urged both the UK and Israeli governments to "avoid pursuing what appear to be party interests over national interests".
Responding in the Commons, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat claimed ministers were "enacting policies that the Foreign Office knows won't work".

He agreed that illegal settlements were wrong and "some Israeli ministers have indulged in hateful propaganda and incitement" but added "this isn't about Israel alone and it certainly isn't about reducing the complexity of the region to a single sentence. Sadly, the government is in the process of doing just that".

Israel's foreign minister Saar also said British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel would be removed, and UK activities to train Palestinian Authority forces in Judea and Samaria - how the Israeli government refers to the West Bank - would be terminated.

Speaking earlier on Tuesday, the country's President Isaac Herzog said the decision would "fall on the wrong side of history", adding: "In the current context, it would be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation."
Herzog said the move would directly harm Palestinians and urged foreign governments to turn towards "constructive dialogue" and cooperation, adding "sanctions are not a solution".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters the White House had no comment on the joint action, adding that "obviously we're not going to do what the UK did".

Earlier, Donald Trump's ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee earlier told the BBC that the US - Israel's most powerful ally - would "without a doubt" respond to the expected sanctions, warning of a "huge economic impact on British businesses".
He suggested action could be taken by individual US states as well as at a central, federal level.
The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people".
As part of the UK announcement, Miliband also announced sanctions on the financing wing of Lebanon's Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group.
New sanctions in line with the US and European Union were also announced on Iran.

The intervention comes almost a year after Sir Keir Starmer's government recognised a state of Palestine, and said the UK had a moral responsibility to support a peaceful future for Israelis and Palestinians.
Israel rejects a two-state solution. It says any final settlement must be the result of negotiations with the Palestinians, and statehood should not be a precondition.
The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Palestinian armed group Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel.
Hamas says that it could accept an interim Palestinian state based on 1967 de facto borders, without officially recognising Israel, if refugees were given the right to return.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.title: PH warns of growing threats to critical undersea infrastructure
articles.summary: Philippine officials are calling for stronger protection of critical undersea infrastructure as submarine cables, energy pipelines, and other maritime systems face growing risks from gray-zone…

blocks.text: Philippine officials are calling for stronger protection of critical undersea infrastructure as submarine cables, energy pipelines, and other maritime systems face growing risks from gray-zone tactics, sabotage, geopolitical tensions, and cyberattacks.
The warning was raised Tuesday, September 8, at the Department of Foreign Affairs-organized Experts’ Forum on Critical International Maritime Infrastructure.

Critical maritime infrastructure includes submarine telecommunications and power cables, pipelines, offshore energy facilities, and other systems that support communications, internet connectivity, energy supply, and economic activity.
The stakes are significant. Submarine telecommunications cables carry more than 99% of international data traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union.
In the Philippines, the Philippine Domestic Submarine Cable Network stretches approximately 2,500 kilometers and links islands from Quezon to Zamboanga.

The Malampaya project, meanwhile, uses a 504-kilometer deepwater pipeline to transport natural gas from its offshore facilities northwest of Palawan to an onshore gas processing plant in Tabangao, Batangas.
Justice Department Chief State Counsel Dennis Chan warned of the potential consequences if such infrastructure were deliberately damaged.

“One can only imagine the scale and gravity of the crisis that our country will be facing if these cables or pipelines are sabotaged. Despite its significance, however, little attention is paid to these cables and pipelines while they silently do their work at the bottom of the seas and the oceans,” Chan said.
Expanding threats
Foreign Affairs Undersecretary for Policy Leo Herrera-Lim said threats to maritime infrastructure have expanded beyond natural disasters and piracy.

“Many of these maritime infrastructures face unprecedented threats. The risks are expanding from traditional natural disasters and piracy to gray zone tactics, state-sponsored cyber attacks, physical sabotage, and the hybrid realities of geopolitical friction,” Herrera-Lim said.
His warning comes as the Philippines continues to face maritime tensions in the West Philippine Sea.
In July, Philippine authorities reported China Coast Guard vessels using water cannons and carrying out dangerous maneuvers against Philippine vessels near Bajo de Masinloc.
The DFA said last week that it had lodged 39 diplomatic protests over China’s actions in the West Philippine Sea so far in 2026.

The DFA stressed that protecting maritime infrastructure is not limited to safeguarding physical assets but also means protecting connectivity, communications, commerce, energy security, and national resilience.
Department of Energy Undersecretary Giovanni Carlo Bacordo identified three major areas of vulnerability: physical and climate risks, geopolitical and regional threats, and cyber threats.
The DOE cited previous cases in which ships’ anchors damaged submarine power cables as an example of the vulnerability of energy infrastructure.
Bacordo said the risks become more serious in contested waters.

“The geopolitical and regional threats. In contested waters, our islands face covert subsea reconnaissance, physical harassment, and exploration and development risks from unauthorized actors,” Bacordo said.
“As we digitalize into smart grids, our remote SCADA networks and offshore substations become prime targets for malicious cyber threats.”
The DOE said the country needs better subsea domain awareness and integrated monitoring systems to detect threats to critical infrastructure, including possible suspicious activity on the seabed.

The Justice Department, meanwhile, raised concerns over whether existing Philippine laws are sufficient to address deliberate attacks on critical underwater infrastructure, particularly when these occur in the country’s exclusive economic zone or continental shelf.

“For submarine cables and pipelines found in our territorial sea and archipelagic waters, hence under the Philippines’ sovereignty, attacks against them can be prosecuted under the Revised Penal Code on damage to property,” Chan said.
The legal situation becomes more complicated farther offshore.

“What appears challenging, however, are attacks on submarine cables and pipelines in our exclusive economic zone and continental shelf, areas not subject to our sovereignty but on which we only exercise sovereign rights under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea,” Chan said.

The DOJ cited as a hypothetical example a foreign fishing vessel deliberately dragging its anchor across the seabed to damage a cable or pipeline, particularly if a civilian vessel were acting under instructions from another state as part of hybrid warfare.

“In such a case, why can’t the coastal state, like the Philippines for that matter, prosecute these foreign offenders directly? This situation highlights the gap and inadequacy of existing laws to deal with these modern problems,” Chan said.

The DOJ has begun institutionalizing a permanent Maritime Advisory and Legal Action Unit that would focus on protecting the Philippine maritime domain through the strategic use of law, including recommending legislation and rules to address gaps in the country’s maritime legal framework.
Philippine officials clarified that the discussions did not identify any particular country as the source of potential threats to critical maritime infrastructure.
Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said the issue should eventually be taken up in broader regional mechanisms.
“This should be incorporated with ASEAN in the East Asia Summit forum, ARF, because this is an issue and a forthcoming issue that will come out,” Lazaro said.
The Philippines is chairing ASEAN in 2026, giving Manila an opportunity to bring maritime infrastructure resilience into regional discussions involving ASEAN and its dialogue partners.

The Experts’ Forum on Critical International Maritime Infrastructure was attended by representatives from countries in the European Union and other allied countries, such as Canada, as well as experts from the Department of Information and Communications Technology and other Philippine agencies. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Smithsonian Institution secretary to retire amid Trump attacks on musuem independence
articles.summary:
‘I have to be honest, it has been stressful,’ Lonnie Bunch III says

The Smithsonian Institution’s secretary, Lonnie Bunch III, will retire at the end of the year amid

blocks.text: The Smithsonian Institution’s secretary, Lonnie Bunch III, will retire at the end of the year amid Donald Trump’s attacks on the museum’s content and independence.

Bunch, who was appointed in 2019 as the first African American to lead the museums, cited personal reasons for departing, while acknowledging the pressure that the president’s attacks on the Smithsonian’s depictions of US history had taken.

“There is no place like the Smithsonian – it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together,” Bunch, 73, said in a statement. “I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.”

“It was really just saying, now’s the time,” Bunch, 73, told the New York Times. He added: “I have to be honest, it has been stressful. And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.”
Trump largely left the Smithsonian alone during his first term, but sought to align its content with his administration’s policies shortly after returning to the White House.

In March 2025, the US president signed an executive order accusing the museum of coming “under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology”, and outlining steps to “restore the Smithsonian Institution to its rightful place as a symbol of inspiration and American greatness”.

Two months later, he tried to fire Kim Sajet as director of the National Portrait Gallery, calling her “a highly partisan person” and a “strong supporter” of the diversity and equity programs his administration was seeking to ban. Bunch pushed back, and the Smithsonian issued a statement affirming that the power to hire and fire lay with him, but Sajet nonetheless resigned in June 2025.
Trump has kept up his pressure campaign in recent months, and in July ordered the National Museum of American History to display signs that accuse it of inaccuracy, though those have yet to appear.
A historian who previously led the creation of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, Bunch acknowledged to the Times that he had to choose his battles in the job.

“My goal has been to win, not to make me feel good,” he said. “To win – to protect the Smithsonian – there were times I would fight, make clear what the red lines were. And there were other times I let things go.”

Bunch’s replacement will be selected by the Smithsonian’s 17-member board of regents, which is led by John Roberts, the chief justice of the supreme court. The panel also includes JD Vance, three Democratic members of Congress and three Republicans, as well as nine private citizens.
Three of those citizens’ terms expired recently, however, and the Trump administration has not yet announced replacements.

Roberts praised Bunch for having “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story”, adding: “The Regents, and the Smithsonian, have benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership. We look forward to working with him in the coming months to ensure a smooth transition for his successor.”

articles.title: US federal court says no constitutional right to clean water in Mississippi case
articles.summary:
Appeals court dismisses lawsuit from Jackson residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their rights

A US appellate court has

blocks.text: A US appellate court has decided that the federal constitution does not guarantee a right to clean water.

That legal opinion came in the form of a decision on Friday from the fifth circuit court of appeals to uphold a lower court’s dismissal of a 2022 lawsuit from several Jackson, Mississippi, residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their constitutional rights.
Those residents of Mississippi’s capital city contended that their local drinking water was unsafe to drink because of high lead levels and other contaminants.

The New Orleans-based fifth circuit’s majority opinion held that the residents wanted “recognition of two new constitutional rights lacking any foundation in the history and tradition of our nation” – those being “the right to be free from exposure to contaminated water and the right to accurate information from public officials”.

In the majority’s view, residents should have gone about their legal fight for clean water another way, such as pursuing “tort claims” or by “electing representatives who will better manage the public-water system, and petitioning their representatives for other remedies”.

Tort claims allege “harms caused by others” while seeking “to impose liability on parties responsible for the harm, and to deter others from committing harmful acts”, according to Cornell University’s law school.

Friday’s decision also said that state and federal officials were working hard to improve the majority-Black city’s drinking water. The residents who filed suit alleged that public authorities had for years failed to mitigate lead levels and failed to inform them about an increase.

“Plaintiffs have not been left to go at it alone,” the court said. “The State of Mississippi and federal government have worked for years, and continue today, to improve the city of Jackson’s drinking water quality through regulations, investigations, and compliance plans.”
Meanwhile, the opinion also said: “It is undisputed that the Constitution does not guarantee clean water.”

The opinion also held that a state doesn’t have a constitutional duty “to provide substantive services for those within its border absent a special relationship”. And municipalities are not constitutionally obligated to provide sewerage, water treatment or waste management services “in a reasonably competent fashion”, the decision said.

The decision nonetheless said that the majority of the court recognized the allegations of “serious government misfeasance” and was “sympathetic to the injuries [the plaintiffs] may suffer as a result”. But, the court’s ruling said “our sympathies cannot be the basis” for converting tort claims into constitutional issues.
“These deprivations, while grievous, do not infringe upon any deeply rooted constitutional right,” the fifth circuit’s opinion said.

Attorneys for the plaintiffs could not immediately be reached for comment. John Horhn, the Jackson mayor, said in a statement: “We are pleased that the fifth circuit upheld the dismissal of these claims.
“The City remains committed to the health, safety, and well-being of every Jackson resident.”
Jackson residents say that they have long reeled from water crises.

The NAACP filed a complaint in September 2022 alleging that Mississippi state authorities violated civil rights law by repeatedly sending federal money earmarked for drinking water safety to white communities rather than Jackson. Such diversion of funds constituted racial discrimination, the complaint said.

“The result is persistently unsafe and unreliable drinking water and massive gaps in the access to safe drinking water that are intolerable in any modern society,” Jackson residents said in a complaint to the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). “Nearly all of the residents of Jackson have watched brackish, dirty, impure, and undrinkable water trickle from their taps. At times, some have had no water at all.”

The NAACP’s Jackson branch sued over the diversion of these funds in August 2025. The suit against several Mississippi state officials alleged that they “intentionally deprived [Jackson] residents … of access to federal relief funds … which were promised to Jackson in order to address the water infrastructure crisis”.

The lawsuit asked for a judge to declare that this diversion of money “is both facially discriminatory and the result of discriminatory purpose” – and to bar officials from permanently siphoning that money away from Jackson.

articles.title: Fourteen go on trial over deadliest Channel small boats disaster
articles.summary: At least 30 men, women and children drowned when their dinghy capsized on 24 November 2021.

blocks.text: Fourteen suspected people smugglers have gone on trial in Paris for their role in the worst ever small boats disaster in the English Channel.
In November 2021, at least 30 men, women and children drowned when their motorised dinghy deflated and started taking on water halfway between France and the UK.
The 14 defendants – mainly Afghan nationals – are accused of manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group.
Most of them deny the charges. Two of the 14, who are alleged to be leaders of the operation, remain on the run and are being tried in absentia.
The boat left the French coast on the evening of 23 November 2021, but ran into difficulty in the middle of the Channel.
One by one the occupants entered the water to try to lessen the weight, but succumbed to the cold and drowned. Only two men survived.
According to the charge sheet, the defendants helped to launch "a small boat of poor quality, unfit to navigate at sea, overloaded and equipped with inadequate life-jackets".
Twenty-seven bodies were found after the boat sank, and another four were confirmed missing.
Many of the people who died were Iraqi Kurds, but others came from Somalia, Ethiopia, Egypt and Afghanistan. The youngest named victim was seven years old.

articles.summary: The victims, employees of an aircraft cleaning company, were in a van when the plane crashed into it

blocks.text: Officials in Florida on Tuesday identified the five people killed in Saturday’s Amazon cargo plane crash at Miami international airport – and said two more remained hospitalized in critical condition.

At a morning news conference, the Miami-Dade sheriff, Rosie Cordero-Stutz, also said both pilots of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767, which careered off the end of the airport’s runway and struck at least two vehicles, were released from the hospital after treatment.
The aircrew, whom she did not name, were the only two people on board.
The sheriff identified Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Narajo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47, as those killed on the ground.

All five dead and the two people most seriously hurt – men aged 79 and 32 – were in a Ford Econoline van that was hit by the aircraft, operated by the all-cargo airline 21 Air llc under contract to Amazon, while it landed after a flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and crashed through fencing on to a roadway.
The victims killed were employees of Professional Ocean Service Corporation, an aircraft contract cleaning company, which released a statement on Tuesday paying tribute to its dead workers.
“Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved,” the statement said.

“Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed. We grieve with those who lost a loved one and pray for the healing and recovery of those who were injured.”
The lives of the families of the victims had been torn apart, Cordero-Stutz told reporters at the news conference.
“[We’re] trying to identify what happened and how it occurred, but for those families, they are going to be living with this for the rest of their lives,” she said.
“So it’s a very difficult time, and it’s very difficult on each and every one of these families.”

Investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) continued their examination of the crash site on Tuesday as the airport began to return to normal operations after three days of cancellations and delays.
At a press conference on Monday afternoon, the NTSB chair, Jennifer Homendy, said teams were working through a scene of “utter devastation” after the crash, which occurred after a thunderstorm.

The aircraft, she said, traveled about 1,300ft beyond the paved surface at the end of the runway and through a perimeter fence. The crash left a wide field of debris, including airbags and other parts of the destroyed vehicles, sections of the aircraft, and fencing.
“It’s pretty extensive,” she said. “Hard to see, and I’m sure it must have been very difficult for the responders as well. I would describe it in one word as devastating, utter devastation.”

Homendy said she planned to give another briefing later on Tuesday that might reveal further details of the accident, retrieved from the plane’s “black box” flight data recorder, which was recovered from the wreckage on Monday.
It is not yet known how fast the aircraft was traveling, but video showed it touched down far along the runway, prompting speculation its speed was too high to be able to stop safely.

Other factors being examined, Homendy said, are weather conditions before and during the landing, and the mechanical condition of the 32-year-old plane that was completing its third flight of the day. Investigators will also want to talk to the two pilots to determine why they decided to proceed with the landing attempt instead of conducting a fly around.
Although the NTSB team would remain on site for about a week, she added, they would focus on recovering as much “perishable” evidence as possible, and not immediately determining a cause.

Some industry experts have said they believe the circumstances of the crash point towards pilot error. They include Robert Clifford, an aviation attorney who has handled cases in numerous commercial aircraft crashes spanning five decades.
“This appears to be a classic tailwind landing mistake where a pilot mistakenly or over-confidently decides to land with a tailwind instead of a headwind,” he said in a statement to the Guardian.
That, he said, “causes excessive touchdown speed and distance from the threshold, leaving inadequate stopping distance for the airplane’s braking and reverse thrust systems to handle”.

Clifford also noted the absence of any arresting devices or fencing at the end of the runway commonly found at other major airports. Homendy said on Monday the NTSB would be looking at that to determine its impact on the severity of the Miami tragedy.

Amazon, meanwhile, said it would work closely with federal investigators on the investigation. Homendy said her team would also examine the relationship between Amazon and 21 Air, the Miami-based aircraft operator.
